title: Failure mode mapping and fast probes for private installs
body:
Purpose:
This is a compact, intentionally messy working note mapping observable failure signals -> likely root causes -> fast probes / commands to run during a first 15–30 minute triage window for VPC / on-prem private deployments. Meant for first responder SREs and solutions engineers. Not a comprehensive playbook; complements the longer runbooks.

Scope and assumptions:
- Applies to private deployments using the Redwood on-prem package or VPC-managed private control plane (k8s + systemd variants).
- Covers common install and runtime failures seen in last 18 months: bootstrap network failures, TF state drift, container/k8s crashes, GPU driver/runtime mismatches, KV cache corruption, and auth/KMS failures.
- Assumes you have kube/ssh access and terraform workspace access.

Quick triage checklist (0–5 mins) 
- Confirm customer impact: are requests failing (400/500), or is cluster degraded but still serving?
- Identify boundaries: control-plane (redwoodctl / API server) vs serving runtime (pods / GPUs) vs infra (networking, storage).
- Grab logs snapshot (one-liners below).

Fast probes (commands to run immediately)
- Control plane health: 
  - curl -fsS http://redwood-controlplane.internal:8080/health || echo "controlplane down"
  - kubectl get pods -n redwood -o wide || kubectl get nodes
  - kubectl logs -n redwood $(kubectl get pods -n redwood -o name | head -n1) --tail=200 | sed -n '1,200p'
- Serving runtime (k8s): 
  - kubectl get pods -n redwood-runtime -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name} {.status.phase}
{end}'
  - kubectl describe pod -n redwood-runtime <pod> | sed -n '1,200p'
  - kubectl logs -n redwood-runtime <pod> -c runtime --tail=300 | sed -n '1,300p'
- Node / GPU checks (ssh into host): 
  - systemctl status redwood-runtime || journalctl -u redwood-runtime -n 200
  - docker ps -a | egrep "redwood|runtime|model"
  - nvidia-smi || /opt/nvidia/bin/nvidia-smi || lsmod | grep nvidia
  - dmesg | egrep -i "oom|nvlink|nvidia|migrat|timeout" | tail -n 80
- Network / DNS / VPC: 
  - iptables -L -n; ip route show; ss -tunlp | egrep ':8080|:9090|:50051'
  - dig +short controlplane.internal || ping -c 3 controlplane.internal
  - traceroute -n controlplane.internal (if cross-AZ latency suspected)
- Storage / mounts: 
  - df -h | egrep '(/mnt/models|/var/lib/docker|/data)'
  - ls -l /mnt/models | head -n 20
- Terraform / state sanity (from operator workstation):
  - terraform workspace show; terraform state list | egrep 'module.runtime|module.controlplane'
  - terraform plan -refresh-only -no-color | sed -n '1,200p'

Signal matrix (observed signal -> probable cause -> first probe)
- "Pods CrashLoopBackOff" -> bad image / missing config / mount permission -> kubectl describe pod; check imagePullBackOff vs crash logs; verify image sha in registry and registry auth logs.
- "Redwood controlplane 502/timeout" -> controlplane overloaded / DB unreachable / stray iptables rule -> curl /health, check postgres process, check cloud SQL connectivity, ulimit, file descriptors.
- "GPU OOM / model eviction" -> model larger than memory or bad quantization -> nvidia-smi, check model size on disk, inspect runtime logs for OOM messages.
- "Bootstrap terraform apply stuck" -> provider auth issue or state lock -> terraform state pull; check S3/GCS lock object; golden command: aws s3api get-object --bucket redwood-tf-state --key workspace/lock || check for DynamoDB state locks.
- "KV cache mismatch / stale responses" -> cache shard mismatch after partial rollout -> restart cache shard, check redis/etcd replication lag, run redis-cli INFO replication.
- "Network blackhole (internal TCP timeouts)" -> security groups, host firewall, MTU mismatch -> iptables -L, tc qdisc show dev eth*, check flannel/calico logs.
- "Auth to KMS failing" -> key policy or VPC endpoint issues -> aws kms decrypt --ciphertext-blob fileb://test || check VPC endpoint routes, security group egress.

Terraform module notes & gotchas (field notes)
- Commonly misconfigured variables:
  - "controlplane_external_hostname" left empty -> TLS cert generation fails, cert-manager won't reconcile. Quick fix: set to known FQDN and re-run cert bootstrap.
  - "ssh_authorized_keys" missing for bastion -> no one can access nodes post-provision. Always validate via terraform output ssh_user and test ssh.
  - "gpu_driver_version" mismatch with AMI -> runtime will install wrong driver or skip install due to package manager differences. Recommend pinning ami + driver combo in module.
- State drift patterns:
  - Users manually modify SG rules or route tables; Terraform apply then tries to revert and sometimes times out. When stuck, use terraform state rm for the resource and re-import after manual fix (document the change).
  - Module versioning: upstream module had provider block changes in v1.3.0 that break older workspaces. Keep a module_version pin in customer manifests.
- Upgrade notes:
  - Plan upgrades in 3 phases: infra (VPC/SGs/db), control plane (k8s CRDs and controllers), runtime (serving binaries and models).
  - Always run canary controlplane rollout to single AZ before full rollout. Use versioned helm charts and do not mix chart versions in one cluster.

Upgrade failure quick-recovery recipe
- If post-upgrade control plane partially fails:
  - Roll back helm release: helm rollback redwood-controlplane <prev-revision> --namespace redwood || restore from backup snapshot (etcd/PG).
  - Reapply any tf changes that were only infra and didn't require control plane changes; avoid reapplying chart-level changes until controlplane healthy.
- If runtime binary causes segfaults on GPU nodes:
  - Scale down serving pool (k8s scale), redeploy older runtime image on a small subset with nodeSelector to validate, then toggle traffic routing.

Common quick remediations (fast wins)
- Recreate a failed pod: kubectl delete pod -n redwood-runtime <pod> --grace-period=0 --force (if transient).
- Rotate service account token if auth failures appear after credential rotation: restart pods that use the token to pick new creds.
- Clear stuck terraform lock: check S3/GCS lock object and DynamoDB; delete lock only if team confirmed.

Hypotheses checklist style (for longer investigations)
- Network: Does packet loss/latency correlate with error windows? Run tcpdump on host ingress and egress.
- Disk/IO: Any IO wait spikes? iostat -xz 5 5 during problem window.
- Resource starvation: top / htop over time; check kube evictions.
- Version mismatch: check runtime binary version vs model runtime expectations (quantization flags, aten version).

Sample troubleshooting timeline for a typical incident (example)
- 00:00–05:00: Validate impact, collect logs, run fast probes above.
- 05:00–15:00: Isolate service boundary; scale down/disable affected routes; start hypothesis testing (network vs infra vs config).
- 15:00–45:00: If not resolved, snapshot state (tf state, etcd), escalate to oncall eng and solutions lead with artifact links.

Escalation rubric
- Page eng-private-deployments when: any upgrade-caused controlplane failure, persistent data corruption, or security/KMS exposure.
- CC product owner + account lead when >30 minutes customer visible outage.

Notes to self / unresolved items (TODOs)
- Build a single script that runs the fast probes and uploads a zipped artifacts bundle to a secure S3 for post-mortem. (Stubbed as bin/collect-private-incident.sh).
- Add health-check endpoints for model-serving pods that expose memory usage and kv-cache hit-rate.
- Check whether module v1.2.3 change to provider block was included in the internal fork; add automated tests that run terraform plan against sample manifests.

Appendix: useful one-liners to paste into Slack during triage
- "Running quick probes: curl controlplane, kubectl get pods -n redwood, nvidia-smi on node, terraform plan -refresh-only; collecting logs to /tmp/incident-<id>.tgz"
- "Action taken: scaled runtime down to 30% to reduce OOM pressure, rolling back controlplane helm release to rev 4"

End of note.

-- A.M. (working draft, will convert into formal runbook after 2 more incidents)
